title: What is the speed of your ideas?
description: We’re taught to believe that great ideas get adopted faster, but this really isn’t true. Why? Ideas change things and most people do not like change. People don’t admit this of course, but watch how people behave and you’ll see it. Most of the time people want security and safety and a great idea will create uncertainty before anything else. We could define a truly great idea as one that’s easy to convince people to use, but this often means only our most convenient ideas go anywhere. Why isn’t this common knowledge? Not sure! I wrote a popular book about the myths of innovation and my theory is we all like to believe we’re pioneers and innovators, even when we’re actually as risk-averse as a pile of rocks . Certainly in the business world executives regularly talk about change… and then change nothing. We’re a funny species really. But it’s our job as designers to help the world, so here we are. One simple way to understand all this is what I call idea velocity. What is idea velocity? Idea velocity is a way to measure how fast ideas move through your workplace. Not just your ideas, all ideas . It’s a way to take yourself out of the equation, at least for a moment, to really see where you are. Some organizations move fast. Most move pretty slow. Where are you? It should be the first question you ask before you come up with ideas for anything. Subscribe now For example, lets take a fictional respected international bank called MegaCrunchBank . Banks are among the most conservative workplace cultures for obvious reasons: they are paid to be reliable and secure above all else. The idea velocity at a bank is very slow . It takes years, and often regulations, for things to change. If Tesla or Marie Curie, or the next super genius creative thinker, worked at a bank, no matter how brilliant they were, change would be slow. There would be dozens of meetings and committee discussions just to update the website. Banks have slow idea velocity and this is true no matter how talented a person is or how great their ideas are. Where is idea velocity fast ? A good example is a three person startup company started by friends. Since they trust each other and there is more work to do than people, everyone is empowered to make decisions. If you volunteered to work on the website, you could have almost any ideas for it and just go make them happen. Why? You’re doing the work. It’s that simple. In short, idea velocity is the existing pace for how ideas become decisions . That pace is shaped by culture and not how great your ideas are. So what does this mean? Designers are often unhappy because we are idea people. We always want high idea velocity. The problem is almost no one else does! Organizations are built to survive, not necessarily to change. Most job functions are there to stabilize things, not to change them. This means it’s critical we measure the pace of change where we are. We must be students of which leaders want a faster pace. Which teams are more ambitious. We need to look at the org chart not in terms of hierarchy but in terms of creative pace and receptivity to changing things. This helps make the system work for you, and not against you . Use idea velocity to help you Once you buy the basic theory of idea velocity, there are ways to use it to your advantage. Here are some questions to help: What is the best example of a big idea leading to change where you work? What can you learn from it? What is an example of a respected leader with a big idea failing to get adoption? What can you learn? Who has the power or influence that allows their ideas to move faster? How can you make them an ally? What is the fastest pace you’ve seen in your organization? Why are you expecting your ideas to move any faster? How can you set realistic expectations of the idea velocity of your team, so you don’t get angry or frustrated for something you can not change? Velocity can increase with momentum. You might need a series of small wins to earn the trust for bigger, faster change. Spend the rest of this week thinking about pace of change. It’s a different and more useful lens for people with ideas.

title: The Personal Brand Trap: Why Humans Shouldn’t Think of Themselves as Brands
description: When I was a wee little boy growing up, I wanted to be a fireman. It seemed considerably more achievable than becoming a ThunderCat or Batman, which were my other career choices when I was eight. At school I had absolutely no clue what I wanted to do as a career. Potentially something arty or sporty, but back in the 90s I was told neither of those were money-makers, so I had to think about getting a proper job. Today, I would classify myself as a designer and educator helping the next generation of creatives build more opportunity for themselves. That feels very aligned with who I am today. But I have also been a barman, factory worker, waiter, tattoo apprentice, window cleaner, failed businessman, unemployable bum, and many other things on the journey to finding this particular version of me. And that is one of the wonderful things about being a human… nobody really freaking knows who they’re going to become. The person you are today is probably very different from the person you were five years ago, and if you’re doing this thing called life properly, there’s a good chance the person you’ll become five years from now will look different again. And, from what my mum tells me… that’s completely normal. Most of us are making it up as we go, collecting experiences and continuously falling forward into newer versions of ourselves… we’re supposed to evolve. So in this little article I want to share my perspective on a topic that I think deserves a little more questioning: personal branding. More specifically, I want to explore why I don’t think humans should think of themselves as brands, and why applying brand logic to a human being can potentially do more harm than good. Thanks for reading The Real Brand Life! Subscribe for free to receive new posts. Now, I’m not here to suggest that personal branding doesn’t exist. That would cause a riot. Instead, I’d like to challenge some of the advice being peddled around willy-nilly on the dopamine drug train that is social media. To do that, I think we first need to agree on the difference between brand logic and human logic. A brand’s job is to reduce complexity. Brands are trying to be recognised at scale and for that to happen, they need to simplify things. They need to make themselves easier to understand, remember and choose. They do that better when they are associated with a couple of very clear ideas. Humans, on the other hand, operate very differently my friends. We change our minds all the freaking time. We become interested in new things. We learn stuff, we grow our minds and then we see the world differently because of it. And an important thing to add is that humans don’t naturally operate at scale. We evolved in small communities and tribes, not in front of thousands of random people online. So if brands become stronger through consistency and humans become stronger through change, are we really sure those two things belong together? That’s why I find phrases like “you are your brand” and “everyone has a personal brand” a little, well… problematic. Being known for something and being a brand are not the same thing. I understand that these phrases are often being used as shortcuts, but even when I account for that nuance, I still think they fundamentally misunderstand what a brand is… and what a human needs. Now, I don’t want this to come across as a rant or a black-and-white argument, as some of the advice coming out of the personal brand camp is incredibly useful. Visibility matters for sure because if nobody knows what the heck you do, how on earth are they supposed to hire you? Other people need to know you exist people. I absolutely believe humans should become known. Known for doing good work, having interesting ideas, standing for something and making a positive impact on the people around them. But becoming known and becoming a product are not the same thing. Being known, or what most would simply call a reputation, is something people gift you over time. It forms through your behaviour and the way you consistently show up for yourself. You don’t have to manufacture it, force it or spend every waking minute trying to manage how you’re perceived by others. A reputation happens naturally as you continue growing into the person you’re becoming. And this is where I think we can run into trouble because the moment we start thinking of ourselves as a brand, our focus can shift. Instead of asking, “Who am I becoming?” we start asking, “How will this look to other people?” The danger is that we start viewing ourselves through the eyes of an audience before we’ve had chance to fully understand ourselves… we start looking at ourselves from the outside in. At first, that might not sound like too much of a problem. In fact, it actually sounds pretty bloody sensible. If you’re running a business, surely you should care about how people feel when they see you. But I don’t believe growth and perception always want the same thing. The thing about growth is that it can look a bit messy from the outside. You change your mind, let go of old ideas and, more often than we’d like to admit, realise you got something wrong. That’s all part of the process. And brand logic doesn’t particularly reward that kind of thinking. Brands gain strength through their consistency. They keep showing up in roughly the same way until people know exactly what to expect from them. And I think that’s where a lot of people can run into a bit of an issue. The more successful a personal brand becomes, the more pressure there can be to keep being the person your audience already knows. To keep talking about the same things, showing up in the same way and feeding the machine that made people pay attention in the first place. That’s the personal brand trap. The human becomes responsible for holding onto a version of themselves they may have already outgrown. And as we see more people choosing freelance careers, building solo businesses and creating opportunities for themselves online, I think this becomes an increasingly important conversation to navigate. I know that perception matters, visibility matters, being known matters, and creating opportunity matters… but so does growth as a human being. Perhaps the challenge isn’t figuring out how to turn people into brands… instead it’s figuring out how to help people become known without trapping them. I’d hate to think that personal branding, the very thing so many people turn to in search of more opportunity, could end up becoming the thing that stops them from becoming who they’re supposed to be. So if I can leave you with a little bit of advice here it would be this: focus on the things you want to be known for, but don’t lose sight of the person you’re becoming along the way. Maybe the goal isn’t to manage perception at all. Perhaps it’s simply to become someone worth paying attention to. Humans are supposed to evolve. Brands are supposed to repeat. The problems arise when we start applying the rules of one to the other, so don’t flatten yourself into a product mindset just because the internet tells you that’s the secret to success. Focus on becoming known for your craft, your kindness and your character. Keep sharing what matters to you because opportunity has a funny way of finding people who do. Just please remember to sprinkle a little patience on yourself along the way. Your mate, James Thoughts on this? Comment below team. I’m excited to hear what you think. title: Default Bias: Who chose your settings?
description: When a choice arrives with one option already set, most people leave it in place, regardless of whether it reflects their actual preference. The friction of changing something, combined with the implicit signal that the pre-set option is normal or recommended, produces consistent gravity toward the status quo. The mechanism runs through several channels at once. Loss aversion makes changing a default feel like risking something already owned. Implied endorsement suggests the default is a reasonable choice, so selecting it requires less justification. And the cognitive cost of evaluating alternatives encourages people to accept the existing state. These forces compound, especially in low-stakes or unfamiliar decisions where people lack strong preferences to override them. Default bias appears across organ donation programs, retirement savings enrollment, privacy settings, and software configuration. In each case, the same population of people produces dramatically different outcomes depending on which option requires action and which requires inaction. The default does not just simplify the interface. It determines the outcome for a large share of users. In design A user opens a new account and immediately lands in a signup flow. Before they have formed any preferences, the product has already decided: marketing emails are on, data sharing is enabled, notifications fire at full volume. The user clicks through, and the defaults stay. Default bias means the designer’s pre-set choices become most users’ permanent choices, whether or not those choices were made with the user’s benefit in mind. This places significant weight on the moment a default is chosen. Every pre-selected option is effectively a policy decision applied to the full user base. Designers who understand this use defaults to serve the majority, while keeping alternatives reachable. Those who ignore it discover that their defaults reflect internal convenience or business incentives rather than user needs. Applications in digital products Set the default communication preference to the least intrusive option, then let users escalate: email digests before individual notifications, not the reverse. When offering a free-to-paid upgrade, pre-select the plan that fits the user’s current usage, not the highest-tier plan, so the default reflects their situation. Place the destructive or irreversible action as the non-default: require an affirmative click to delete, unsubscribe, or share data, rather than treating those as pre-selected states. In onboarding forms, default empty fields to blank rather than placeholder values that users might submit without reading. On privacy and data settings, default to the most private configuration and present expansion as a deliberate user choice, not a correction of a setting they already “agreed to.” When a setting has a best-fit value for most users, pre-select it with a visible label like “Recommended” so the default carries transparent reasoning rather than hidden authority. Industry examples Countries with automatic organ donation enrollment see consent rates above 90%. Countries that require a positive registration act see rates below 20%. Same populations, different defaults. Thaler and Benartzi documented a similar pattern in 401(k) enrollment in 2003. Companies that switched retirement plans to automatic enrollment saw participation jump from around 50% to over 90%. Employees could still remove themselves. Most did not. Microsoft pre-selected telemetry and automatic update settings in Windows 10 that collected substantial user data. Changing them required navigating several menus. Few users did. Google enabled AI-assisted email completion in Gmail by default for all users. Adoption was high not because users chose it, but because disabling it required a deliberate action most skipped. Apple’s App Tracking Transparency, released in 2021, shifted ad tracking from an on-by-default state to an explicit prompt. Consent rates dropped from an estimated 70% to under 30%. No one changes what they don’t notice Changing a default requires two things most people avoid at the same time: forming a preference and acting on it. The pre-set option eliminates both requirements. People accept it without deliberating, often without noticing the choice was made. This is not a failure of attention, rather a rational response to cognitive load . When a decision is low-salience and the default seems reasonable, the cost of evaluating alternatives outweighs the benefit. The designer who sets the default has, in effect, already made the decision for the majority. This is why defaults carry ethical weight. A designer can claim to offer choice while structuring the choice so that most users never exercise it. Defaults are most powerful in one-time setup flows, where users move quickly and rarely return to revisit. Designers who want users to engage with settings should surface them at the moment of relevance, not bury them in preferences menus users open once and forget. Choosing the default is unavoidable. There is no neutral pre-selection. Every product that ships with a setting in place has already made a choice about whose interests that setting serves. Further reading The Power of Defaults — Jakob Nielsen, Nielsen Norman Group (2005) Defaults — The Decision Lab Status Quo Bias — The Decision Lab Choice Architecture 2.0: How People Interpret and Make Sense of Nudges — Job Krijnen, Behavioral Scientist (2018) Defaults Are Not the Same by Default — Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber, and Johnson, Behavioral Scientist (2019) You just read why the pre-set option wins. So here’s one I’ve set for you: The reference designers keep open. Default Bias is 1 of 106 principles in Psychology of Design; the complete reference behind this newsletter. What attention does. How trust forms. Why habits stick. Each one written the way you just read this one: the mechanism, where it shows up, and how to use it. Filter by cluster, jump to the principle you need, ship something that fits how people are wired. Get Psychology of Design

title: leia se você tiver múltiplos interesses ☕️🐢
description: Parte da minha família veio à Espanha para ficar uns dias perto de mim e da minha filhinha. Pra estar mais presente, abri o meu túnel do tempo e escolhi uma edição antiga pela qual tenho muito carinho :¬) Espero que você goste tanto quanto a Eleninha gostou dos desenhos de fruta que fizemos! É possível ser multipotencial, mas finalizar projetos? É possível focar, mas sem deixar a sua natureza curiosa de lado? Depois de aaanos frustrado , aprendi alguns caminhos que me fazem dizer “sim” para as perguntas acima. Nessa edição, queria dividir um deles com você :¬) O ministério da criatividade “a diverte”: isso não é uma fórmula pronta. Cada pessoa e projeto tem um contexto diferente. O texto não contém glúten - mas, como tudo na internet, não é para todo mundo, nem para todo tipo de projeto. Acho bonito pensar em projetos como sementinhas que precisam de diferentes níveis de nutrição. E como essas sementes se alimentam de recursos super valiosos - seu tempo, dinheiro e energia - é muito sensato que a gente cuide deles com carinho. Você já deve ter ouvido 1004 vezes que definir prioridades é importante. Mas se, assim como eu, você também tem múltiplos interesses e ideias, considera fazer isso dessa forma: Transformar em prioridade só aquilo que você poderia sustentar numa semana ruim (uma hipótese inicial que pode ser ajustada, claro). Criar uma linha do tempo e inserir os [1] projetos atuais (prioridades) e [2] projetos futuros. Por que recomendo isso? :¬) Parece bobo: mas isso traz clareza visual sobre onde (e por quanto tempo) você pensa em investir seus recursos. Mas isso NÃO quer dizer que você precisa deixar sua curiosidade de lado e esquecer dos futuros projetos, viu? Não é uma escolha binária. Por que? :¬) Porque, felizmente, o processo criativo é composto por etapas diferentes. Deixar ideias marinando e construir um acervo de referências também é parte do processo criativo, concorda? E o mais legal: Essas partes do processo podem fluir espontaneamente: quando esbarramos com novidades, notamos algo ao redor, fazemos associações aleatórias, etc. E por que isso é lindo? Isso permite nutrir as sementes do futuro com leveza - sem desviar seus recursos das prioridades que você definiu. Nem tudo é 8 ou 80. Nem tudo é preto ou branco. Um jardim cresce com ritmos diferentes. “E, na prática… o que você faz, Tiagão? Gosto do Bulbassauro, mas chega de analogia com planta.” Projetos atuais: transformar em hábitos. Algo sustentável, que cabe na sua rotina. Esse vídeo ajuda com isso. Futuros projetos: ir salvando referências, anotações e links em pastinhas separadas; em algum momento, você-do-futuro vai transformá-las em prioridade :¬) Começar algo novo = um prêmio. E, agora, você começa com a confiança de que aprendeu a usar o ponto final. E, por último, mas não menos importante: É essencial – e uso essa palavra com muita intenção – lembrar que: As ideias-que-você-ainda-não- começou vão parecer “perfeitas” na sua imaginação… até você botar a mão na massa. É na hora da fazeção que a gente encontra os desconfortos, desafios e as imperfeições. Esse constraste faz a gente desistir de ideias, mesmo que ainda fizesse sentido terminá-las. Por isso, sugiro se preparar (antes!) para o inevitável canto das sereias. P.S. Se esse texto ajudar UM ser vivo do Sistema Solar, eu já fico feliz. P.P.S. Já me frustrei (muito!) por achar que focar = ignorar a minha natureza curiosa e multipotencial. Por isso, torço para que você vá nutrindo o seu jardim e, aos pouquinhos, comece a tirar as suas ideias do papel :¬) 🥕 o melhor bolo de cenoura era o da minha avó. 🎾 uma curadoria de joguinhos para substituir redes sociais. 🌍 um jogo divertido para aprender sobre a geografia da África. 👀 eu queria tanto ter criado isso aqui. 🐦 curti as brisas visuais do Adam. Esse é um pum sobre assinaturas. Estou num momento de questionar o que assino ( streaming , apps , etc.) para cancelar ou inserir coisas novas. Como você e muita gente que lê a news podem curtir assuntos parecidos, queria te perguntar: Quais das suas assinaturas valem muuuito a pena no seu contexto? Aquela que você paga, com prazer, todo mês ou todo ano? Por que? :¬) Deixe um comentário Com carinho, Tiago 🐢

description: De tempos em tempos gosto de escrever uma edição bem aleatória. Como estamos em setembro, o mês 9, trouxe 9 comentários e assuntos que dificilmente terei contexto pra compartilhar. P.S. Se estiver sem ideias, abre o teclado de emojis do celular. Emojis sobre assuntos aleatórios em um espaço pequenos de tempo ajuda muito a lembrar de histórias! Com carinho, Tiago 🐢

title: sua geladeira ☕️🐢
description: A gente cozinha com os ingredientes que estão na nossa geladeira. “Ai, ai, ai… Lá vem o Tiago com outra analogia que envolve comida....” Mas falando sério: isso não rima com o processo criativo? Pensa só: os ingredientes são o nosso repertório e a geladeira é a nossa cachola :¬) Ou seja, guardamos as referências e vivências de forma intencional (ou subconsciente) por lá. Um dos maiores desafios de seres humanos que habitam o Sistema Solar em 2026 é não deixar que os algoritmos das redes sociais sempre façam as compras. Afinal, a rotina é corrida! Deixá-los escolher por nós deixa tudo tão fácil e conveniente , não é? Eles já sabem do que a gente gosta. É só se deixar levar. Não precisa pensar ou gastar energia pra consumir. E como toda “bolha” tem ingredientes parecidos, a gente acaba provando uma variedade pequena de pratos. [ esse brinquedo de comidinhas de madeira é da Elena - e é muuuito divertido! ] Mudar o nosso consumo impacta diretamente no que a gente pensa, sente e cria. O processo criativo não começa na cozinha: ele envolve a escolha do mercado, o tempo que ficamos nele e os ingredientes novos que a gente escolhe experimentar :¬) garimpos 🦭 eu e você já temos conexão pelo LinkedIn ? :) 🐬 mais uma curadoria de músicas de fases aquáticas de videogame. 💧 falando em água: essa instalação artística é tão simples, mas tão legal. 🐙 se você curte branding, criatividade e desconfia de quem fala sobre o “jeito certo” de fazer as coisas, acho que você vai curtir esse livro. pum Esse pum é um eco do texto ali de cima :¬) Tenho brisado muito sobre o quanto cada pessoa que sigo me inspira a [1] comprar coisas ou a [2] criar coisas. [ Sempre que escrevo “coisa” penso que queria ter crescido em Minas e usar a palavra “trem”. ] Não que o consumo seja inerentemente ruim, tá? Mas acho tão perigoso quando os nosso algoritmos começam a nutrir o nosso cérebro sobre como viver uma vida aesthetics , prazerosa e interessante quase sempre a partir do que podemos (ou não) comprar. Se perdendo nessa bolha, é fácil esquecer como a sua autoexpressão criativa - seja por fotografia, desenho, escrita, etc. - também molda o seu estado interno e externo. As pessoas que mais te inspiram têm feito você querer criar mais ou comprar mais? E, pra você, qual é o limite saudável entre esses dois? P.S. Lembrando que não é um papo binário e com resposta de múltipla escolha - é só um convite pra gente pausar e pensar :¬) Com carinho, Tiago 🐢

title: Why CEOs ignore design leaders
description: Designers have big egos. There, I said it. An ego is a sense of self, and creative people need strong ones to have faith in their ideas. But ego is dangerous and can get in the way of just about everything else. I chose to make the first part of Why Design Is Hard directly about the designer ego trap , and how blind designers are to our self-defeating behavior. We spend too much time with other designers who have similiar egos and personalities which means we’ve spent decades sharing our complaints into an echo chamber of learned helplessness. The reason CEOs ignore design leaders is simple: CEOs ignore almost everyone . That’s their job. Can you imagine what their schedule looks like? VPs ignore almost everyone too. Why? The entire organization is competing for their attention. Every person in every job has their own agenda and wants to influence the VP to get it. To be a good executive means intentionally limiting who can influence you and how they can do it. If you feel ignored, here is the best advice: be curious, not judgmental. Judgement keeps you where you are but complaints alone are not effective arguments . Remember that curiosity is your superpower as a designer and it will find you a way forward. You are being judgmental and egocentric if you say: My CEO is an idiot (even if it’s true, so what? This can be an advantage) Why I am not involved more? Why do they hate designers? Why do they dislike me personally? Why don’t THEY get it ? Why I am an always on the outside? These are all EGO centered questions. These questions are entirely centered on YOU. And it’s no surprise that when you raise complaints like this you are probably seen as being self-involved. CEOs hear selfish complaints all day long from directors and other executives and it’s exhausting. As much as you’re rightfully frustrated, much of your peer group in other roles are frustrated too and voicing similiar complaints for more power. No department head shows up and says “Hey CEO! Cut my team in half please. We’re just not that important.” They are always demanding something. CEOs and VPs tune out much of the complaining as static. They have to. Design culture has normalized the belief that these complaints have any effect and it’s a terrible mistake. To be more effective you must act on curiosity and instead ask: Maybe there are good reasons great design is not a strategy where I work ? If I’m left out, who is on the inside and how did they get there? What can I learn? How can I partner with them? What is a better promise I can make to solve important problems for powerful people? What do I not understand about how things really get done where I work? What am I willing to change in myself to have more influence without my workplace changing? Or what do I need to accept about the limits of my role ? One major hypocrisy of designers is we claim superiority at understand people, but then fail to study our own coworkers to better understand them. We just let our egos focus on blame instead, which leads nowhere . The above list is simple, actionable questions, but design culture does not embrace them yet. Good questions lead to discoveries. Simply by reaching out to people with curiosity you will get more useful responses. For example, to say “Hey Sally, as the VP of engineering, I can help your team be more efficient, but I’m not involved early enough to help. What advice do you have for me?” Is a request for involvement combined with an offer to help solve a problem. This will always be more effective than demanding involvement in anything because of your job title (which designers have a long history of doing). Subscribe now But these ego habits are hard to shake . The response this book and the dozens of talks I’ve given on it is often, “why should I have to do this?” And my answer is you don’t! But if you are miserable it is you who has to change something. No one is going to do it for you. It could be to accept how organizations tend to work and stop dreaming of design nirvana. It might be realizing you are competing for influence with powerful people and it’s a skill to learn. Or perhaps it’s to reevaluate where you expect creative satisfaction to come from and seek it somewhere outside of your job. But all three require moving past the limitations of ego and to open your eyes. Related posts: Escape the design ego trap The system can work for you What is the speed of your ideas in your workplace? The fun way to gain influence Or trust me and get my book, Why Design Is Hard

title: What is "the gravity of average" and why is it holding you back?
description: I grew up believing one thing: Don’t be average. Looking back now, as an older, slightly fatter man, there’s something wonderfully ironic about that particular piece of advice. While every person in authority was telling me not to become average, the systems around me were teaching me exactly how to become it. School teaches us there was one right answer. Business teaches us there’s a right process. Algorithms tell us there’s a right format. Most industries have their own best practices, and society at large constantly reminds us that fitting in is safer than standing out. None of these proven systems are bad. In fact, they’re incredibly useful. They help us educate millions of little people, build reliable businesses, and make sense of an increasingly complicated world. But when you start stacking them on top of one another, year after year, decade after decade… something intriguing happens. They all pull us in the exact same direction: Toward what’s proven Toward what’s predictable Toward what’s familiar Toward the flipping middle We hear a lot these days about falling test scores, declining creativity, and a lack of ambition. I’m not convinced that’s the whole story. I think we’re living inside an ecosystem of invisible forces that constantly reward the safest path. Millions of perfectly sensible decisions, made by perfectly sensible people, combine to suck us toward the same ideas until we all end up in the exact same place… the fookin’ middle. I call this: the gravity of average. Whether we realize it or not, we’ve been caught in its invisible pull since the day we were born… damn it. Here are the five layers of gravity conspiring against us all, and why you need to fight them with everything you’ve got to protect your individual magic. 1. Educational gravity Our first experience of this gravity starts in the classroom. School has an incredibly difficult job: educating millions of children fairly and consistently, often with limited resources and enormous expectations. The only way to make that possible is to rely on standardized curricula, rigid grading schemes, and easily measured outcomes. From a very young age, we learn to optimize for what gets rewarded … the gold stars, the praise from teachers, the good-old pats on the back. Before long, we’re no longer just learning the subject, we’re learning how to succeed within the system. The educational environment doesn’t intentionally produce average people. Far from it. But when success is measured in the exact same way for everyone, it’s only natural that millions of children begin chasing the exact same things. The more people optimize for the identical outcome, the more they will eventually look alike… it’s the logical outcome of a predictable system. 2. Economic gravity Businesses only exist if they survive, and to do that, they have to make rational decisions. If a pricing model has worked before, why change it? If a marketing strategy has proven successful, why reinvent it? If a competitor is growing using a particular approach, it’s only natural to copy it. None of these are bad decisions. Economist Harold Hotelling described this exact phenomenon in what became known as Hotelling’s Law . When businesses compete for the same customers, they naturally drift toward one another rather than away. Differentiation feels risky, while similarity feels sensible. Over time, this way of thinking compounds. What starts as “best practice” gradually becomes the default way of doing business. When an entire industry chases the identical measures of success (revenue, profit, or market share), even the most original business ideas eventually drift toward the average when they optimize for the same thing. 3. Social gravity As humans, we’ve always worried about belonging. For most of human history, being accepted by the group dramatically increased our chances of not becoming dead. That instinct is still hardwired into us. One of my favourite psychology experiments that backs this up comes from Solomon Asch . Participants were invited into a room to complete what they thought was a simple test about the length of a few lines. What they didn’t know was that everyone else in the room was an actor hired to be in on the experiment. The answers were obvious, but one by one, the actors deliberately gave the wrong answer. Faced with an entire room disagreeing with them, many participants ignored what they could clearly see and went along with the crowd instead. Around 75% of people conformed at least once, even though the group was clearly wrong. Nobody has to tell us to fit in. We just learn which parts of ourselves earn acceptance and which parts are safer left hidden. 4. Algorithmic gravity Welcome to the newest kid on the block. Algorithms don’t care about “silly” things like originality… all they give a poop about is retention. The easiest way to predict what will keep your attention is to look at what has already worked. Successful ideas become recommendations. Recommendations become trends. Trends become the templates that every influencer and their dog starts copying. Before long, thousands of people are creating different versions of the exact same thing because that’s what the system keeps serving up. Social media isn’t in the business of finding the next brilliant idea. It’s in the business of keeping us scrolling, and scrolling, and scrolling. And the easiest way to do that is by feeding us a slightly repackaged version of the average… the baseline of everything the system has already gobbled up before. 5. Professional gravity Every profession develops its own “playbook.” Designers have processes, marketers have foolproof plans, and consultants have their frameworks. Most of these defaults exist because someone, at some point, solved a real problem for a real person… hurrah. The danger happens when best practice subtly becomes the only practice. The longer an approach survives unquestioned, the more it feels like common sense. Before long, entire industries are repeating formulas that worked 30 years ago, even though the world has completely evolved around them. The comfort zone is a very dangerous place. Nothing grows there, as they say. The optimization trap What I’ve realized about these five forces is that they all share the exact same mischievous mechanism. Every system must decide what success looks like and, once it does, the rest of us naturally optimize for it. School rewards grades. Business rewards revenue. Algorithms reward engagement. Society rewards acceptance. Professions reward best practice. None of the above are bad… but when millions of people chase the exact same measures of success, gravity takes over. Human beings are remarkably good at adapting to their environment. The more we align ourselves with the same definition of success, the more we begin to resemble one another. And today, more people than ever are finding themselves in the middle. For most of history, becoming competent at something took years of deliberate practice. Today, technology can get almost anyone to “good enough” in a matter of minutes. Technology is closing the gap from below, while optimization is closing the gap from above. People who once struggled to produce competent work can now create something perfectly passable with better tools. At the same time, many of the people who were once exceptional are handing more of their thinking over to those same tools. In the pursuit of speed they often sacrifice the originality and personality that made them stand out in the first place. One force lifts people into the middle. The other pulls people back towards it. Now, there is absolutely nothing wrong with being average. Millions of people build fulfilling careers, do meaningful work, and live brilliant lives without ever trying to stand out. But commercially, today, average is becoming a far riskier place to build a future. To riff on something Rory Sutherland once said: when you become logical, you become predictable. And when you become predictable, you become replaceable. That doesn’t mean you should reject logic or stop using new technology. It simply means those things are no longer enough. They help you meet the standard, yes, but they’ll never make you the obvious choice. I’ve come to believe that opportunity doesn’t flow toward the middle. It flows toward recognizable differences that people trust. The gravity of average never disappears. You simply decide whether to drift with it… or spend your time pushing against it. Maybe that’s what Mr. Hotelling was trying to tell us all along. Test the edges. - James This article first appeared in my Fast Company column. You can check it out here .

title: Objects Quarterly
description: Welcome to the latest edition of OBJECTS QUARTERLY, a roundup of object-related items of interest published, uh, quarterly, for supporters of The Art of Noticing. Attending to objects is a sub-theme of TAoN, and a favorite subject of mine. Revisit prior OQ issues, and other mindful materialism posts, here . Enjoy ! Via Wikipedia . By Arpingstone - Arpingstone, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=38786 “KIM’S GAME” Today I have another object-centric attention game borrowed from fiction — borrowed twice over, in fact. It comes from a short story callled “ Kim’s Game, ” by Sadia Shepard, published in The New Yorker earlier this year. In the story, a character recalls a childhood game that his father evidently took from Rudyard Kipling’s Kim : “My father would arrange a handful of objects on a tray—an old coin, a ribbon, a rock, a thimble, that sort of thing—and ask me to memorize them. Then he’d cover the tray with a newspaper and ask me to describe what I remembered. Sometimes, he’d take something away to see if I noticed . In the Kipling novel, the game is part of Kim’s training to be a spy.” This turns out to have become a well-known game , played (with variations) by children, the Cub Scouts , the military, and others. It actually sounds like a fun exercise — and also potentially a great assignment, particularly for a writing class. (And for the record it does sound like decent spy training, too.) If you try it, or have played it in the past, tell me about it! And as always I welcome your object-centered attention games, from fiction or real life. description: Se a comparação nas redes sociais afeta a sua confiança e autoestima: Considera ler esse texto sem glúten e escrito com muito carinho? :¬) Essa edição foi criada de um café bonitinho enquanto escutava música melancólica porque minha mãe/irmãs (que estavam me visitando) acabam de voltar da Espanha. O saldo de hoje foi de dois cafés com leite, um bolinho de limão e mais parágrafos que o normal. Ontem, vi um vídeo de um moço fazendo 14 barras e mostrando a porcentagem da população que faz 1, 4, 9,(…),14 repetições. E (assim como você?) eu imaginei que os comentários teria muita gente contando que consegue fazer mais de 14 repetições. Esse achismo tem nome: Viés de sobrevivência. Ele é uma ilusão de ótica lógica que explica (muito!) sobre o comportamento de humanos que vivem no Planeta Terra e têm um celular na mão. Como ele funciona? :¬) Bora simular um cenário fictício com uns números chutados? 1000 pessoas veem o vídeo onde o moço faz 14 barras. 1 dessas 1000 pessoas já fez mais que 14 barras. Essa pessoa comenta no vídeo: afinal, ela se sente confortável e feliz de compartilhar isso. As 999 pessoas que fazem menos de 14 barras são a maioria; mas elas se sentem menos à vontade e têm menos motivação de se expressar por não pertencer ao “Grupo 14+”. Resultado: a seção de comentários mostra, em maioria, pessoas que podem fazer mais de 14 barras: uma proporção bem distorcida! O mesmo rola quando se fala sobre salário e faturamento pela internet. É raro ouvir gente que ainda não ganha um número “alto” (entre aspas por ser muito relativo) abrindo essa informação. O ministério da escrita adverte: exceções existem e a gente está falando de cenários mais comuns/prováveis. Quanto mais alguém se sente acima da média em um aspecto da sua vida, mais à vontade ela fica de mostrá-lo. Quanto mais estímulos acima da média nós vemos, mais achamos aquilo normal. Quando normalizamos o excepcional , aumentamos a chance de nos sentir atrasados ou inferiores. Em 2 minutos online , você já viu o pace da Laura, os look do João, o trabalho da Fê, as viagens da Lu e o garimpo novo do apê do Miguel. Nesses 2 mins, de forma subconsciente , você sente que não viaja o suficiente e que precisa ganhar mais. E, pô, melhorar na corrida, né? Deixar sua casa mais bonita, etc. Esses 120 segundos escalam. Ele se desdobra no seu tempo de tela diário e tuuuudo isso vira uma bola de neve. Resumindo: qual é o desafio? Se o nosso feed é feito de recortes acima da média, o nosso parâmetro do normal é distorcido e reajustado sem a gente perceber. Racionalmente e, na teoria , é fácil concordar que isso tudo acontece. Na prática , como o nosso consumo rola no piloto automático, a gente não lembra que está vendo apenas os “sobreviventes”. As exceções. Uma ferramenta pra ajudar a resolver: Espero (de coração!) que nomear e entender o “viés de sobrevivência” insira uma ferramenta no seu repertório. E torço pra que ela seja um dos caminhos que, aos poucos, possa te ajudar a lidar melhor com a comparação. Com carinho, Tiago 🐢 🌍 essas colagens digitais em 3D tão maravilhosas! 👀 ameeeei esse projetinho feito à mão pra prateleiras! 🎾 eu adoro escutar as entrevistas desse canal (em inglês). 🥕 escrevi essa edição ouvindo esse álbum melancólico (minha família acabou de ir embora depois de me visitar aqui na Espanha). Esse é um pum sobre elogios aleatórios :¬) Há uns 16 anos, um amigo meu disse que eu era MUITO bom em pedir pizza por telefone. A gente se encontrava 1x por semana na casa dele pra fugir do trânsito pós trabalho. Era muita gente e várias pizzas ”meio X, meio Y”, sabe? Então criei uma forma de organizar tudo e pedir mais rápido. Uma habilidade que nunca vai aparecer no meu currículo, portfolio e, provavelmente, não vou ter outra chance pra contar. Qual foi o elogio mais aleatório que você já recebeu na vida? Um abração, Tiago 🐢

This subject of re-reading books has popped up randomly a couple of times for me lately, and made me think about how long it’s been since I’ve done it. I guess I now worry that I just don’t have enough time to repeat a book when there are so many I haven’t read once! That said, the most recent was The Ladies’ Paradise , by Zola, which I read for a second time about 10 years ago. The book I’ve read the most times is Native Son , three times (all in my 20s, I believe). What about you? Love to hear your thoughts! title: Live event: Design Courage, with Bob Baxley
description: I’m excited to invite you to join me for this live event next week. What: Design Courage: Bob Baxley When: Wednesday, August 26 · 4:00pm PT Where: here on Substack No one is coming to champion your work. Not your manager, not your CEO, not the industry. Every designer figures this out eventually, usually the hard way. Bob Baxley has spent 35 years leading design at Apple, Yahoo!, Pinterest, and ThoughtSpot, and he’s one of the few people in this field willing to say plainly that courage — not craft, not process — is the scarcest resource in design. He’s joining me live for a conversation about Design Courage: How to Be Your Own Champion , where we will explore true tales of designers who took real risks on real projects. I’ll be interviewing Baxley in what will be a fun and interactive format. We’ll get into knowing when you own a decision versus merely advise on it, how to push back on executives in ways that build credibility instead of burning it, and where to find nerve when the org isn’t asking you for any. Bring your questions. We’ll have time. Hope to see you.
